title: What does the problem cost?
principle: Ask what the problem costs them before you show the fix.

screens.text: Let me tell you about a long study. British researcher Neil Rackham and his team studied more than 35,000 sales calls in 23 countries over 12 years. They wanted to know what the best sellers did differently in big sales.

screens.prompt: What do you think the best sellers did more than the others?

options.label: Offered a lower price to buyers

screens.why: They asked questions, especially about how much the buyer's problems cost them. Many people think good sellers talk a lot. But asking the right questions mattered more.

screens.title: SPIN questions
screens.text: Rackham called the four kinds of questions SPIN. Situation: ask for facts. Problem: ask what goes wrong. Implication: ask what the problem costs. Need-payoff: ask how fixing it would help. In big sales, Implication questions mattered most because they showed the full cost of a problem.

screens.prompt: You ask a café owner, "When snacks run out at 5 pm, how many customers leave?" Which kind of question is this?
screens.why: Right. You already know his snacks run out. Now you are asking how many customers he loses because of it. This is an Implication question.

wrong.a: A Situation question asks for facts, like "How many snacks do you sell?" This question asks how many customers he loses when snacks run out. That's an Implication question.
wrong.b: A Problem question asks what goes wrong, like "Do snacks run out?" You already know they do. Asking how many customers leave is an Implication question.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: Rackham studied sales to big companies, but you can ask the same questions at a café. Remember the café owner who said, "I will surely buy," but never ordered? It's February, and you visit him again. Each brownie costs you ₹20 to make.

screens.prompt: Here are four questions for the café owner. Put them in the order you would ask them, with the first question at the top.
steps: How many snacks do you sell each evening?
Do your snacks ever run out early?
When they run out, how many customers walk away?
How would it help you if the shelf stayed full until 9 pm?
screens.why: Good. First ask for facts. Then ask what goes wrong and how much it costs. Last, ask how fixing it would help. This helps the owner see why he needs your brownies.

screens.prompt: About 15 customers leave each evening. Each would spend about ₹60. How much sales money does he lose in a 30-day month?
screens.why: Right. 15 customers × ₹60 = ₹900 in lost sales each evening. Over 30 evenings, that's ₹27,000 in lost sales. He had not counted this before. Now he can see how much the problem costs him.

wrong.a: ₹900 is the sales he loses in one evening: 15 × ₹60. For 30 evenings, multiply ₹900 × 30. That's ₹27,000 in lost sales.
wrong.c: ₹6,300 is for one week: ₹900 × 7. But the question asks about 30 days. ₹900 × 30 = ₹27,000.

screens.prompt: You want to know what really happened, not what the owner thinks he might do. Which question should you ask?

options.label: How many evenings did snacks run out last week?
Would you buy brownies from me each day?
Do you think your café needs more brownies?

screens.why: Right. This is the Mom Test from Unit 2. Ask what happened last time. Asking about last week gives you facts. Then ask how much those evenings cost him.

wrong.b: He may say yes just to be polite. That does not prove he will buy. Remember the Mom Test from Unit 2: ask what happened last week, not what he might do.
wrong.c: Your question suggests the answer you want. He may agree just to be polite. Remember the Mom Test from Unit 2: ask what happened last week.

screens.setup: It's late February. The owner has ten minutes for you. About 15 customers leave each evening when snacks run out. You want ₹45 for each brownie. His current snack supplier charges ₹30. You have brought a box of brownies.
screens.question: What will you do in those ten minutes?

options.label: Show your brownies first, then explain the recipe
options.outcome: He tastes a brownie and smiles. "Very nice. Let me think about it." Your ten minutes end before you ask about his lost sales. A week later, he still has not called.
options.why: You showed him your brownies before asking about his problem. He liked the taste but did not see how your brownies could help his business.
options.better: First ask how much he loses when snacks run out. Then show your brownies.

options.label: Ask when snacks run out, then show your brownies
options.outcome: He calculates his lost sales: about ₹27,000 a month. Then you show your brownies. He orders 10 brownies a day for a two-week trial at ₹45 each. You keep ₹25 per brownie, or ₹250 a day.
options.why: He calculated the ₹27,000 in lost sales himself. Now he sees how your brownies could help him reduce that loss.

options.label: Match his supplier's price, then show your brownies
options.outcome: He agrees to buy 10 brownies a day at ₹30 each. You keep only ₹10 per brownie, or ₹100 a day. He now sees you as a low-price baker.
options.why: His problem costs him ₹27,000 in lost sales, but you focused on price. You now earn less than half of what you could earn at ₹45 per brownie.
options.better: First ask how much he loses when snacks run out. Then show your brownies.

screens.text: Before you show how you can help, ask what the ___ costs the buyer. Then ___ more than you talk.
screens.why: Right. Rackham's best sellers asked Implication questions and listened. The café owner calculated his own ₹27,000 in lost sales. That helped him see why he needed your brownies.

summary: SPIN has four kinds of questions: Situation, Problem, Implication and Need-payoff. Implication questions ask how much a problem costs.
When buyers calculate how much a problem costs, they can see why paying for your help makes sense.
Ask what happened last time. Then listen more than you talk.

cards.front: "When the machine breaks, how many orders do you lose?" What kind of SPIN question is this?
cards.back: Implication. It asks how many orders the buyer loses because of the problem.

cards.front: 15 customers leave each evening. Each would spend ₹60. How much sales money is lost over 30 days?
cards.back: ₹900 in lost sales each evening × 30 = ₹27,000 in lost sales a month.

cards.front: You have ten minutes with a buyer. What comes first?
cards.back: Ask questions first. Help the buyer see how much the problem costs before you offer a fix.
